cues.text: A Fatherless Farm Boy
Born in 1815 at Becchi, a hillside hamlet near Turin, John Bosco lost his father before he turned two, leaving his mother, Margaret, to raise three sons in poverty.
Even as a boy tending sheep, John displayed a natural gift for holding other children's attention.
He entertained them with tricks and acrobatics learned from traveling performers, then repeated, word for word, the sermon he had heard at Mass that day.
A Vow to the Streets
Ordained a priest in Turin in 1841, John's ministry began almost by accident.
On 8 December 1841, he met a poor orphan named Bartolomeo Garelli in a sacristy.

Discovering the boy knew nothing of the faith, he resolved to prepare him for his First Communion — the seed of what became a lifelong mission to the abandoned, working-class boys flooding into industrializing Turin.
The Oratory at Valdocco
John gathered growing numbers of street boys for religious instruction, games, and eventually shelter, settling his work at Valdocco, then a poor suburb of Turin.

His own mother, 'Mama Margaret,' joined him there, giving the last ten years of her life — including selling her own furniture and jewelry — to caring for the boys who filled what became the first Salesian home.
A New System of Education
John developed and refined what became known as the Salesian preventive system .
He deliberately rejected the corporal punishment common in the era's schools, instead surrounding boys with positive environments, frequent confession and Communion, and patient, fatherly guidance.
This approach was meant to prevent wrongdoing rather than merely punish it after the fact.
He also insisted on teaching boys practical trades, becoming an early pioneer of vocational education for the urban poor.
Founding the Salesians
In 1859, John formally organized his collaborators into a religious congregation, the Society of St.
Francis de Sales (the Salesians), receiving full papal approval in 1869.
By the time of his death, the order had grown from its original seventeen members to 773, with foundations across Italy, Spain, France, England, and South America.
John also co-founded, with St.
Maria Domenica Mazzarello, a corresponding congregation of women religious devoted to poor girls.
Legacy
John Bosco died at Turin in 1888, and was canonized in 1934 by Pope Pius XI.
His enduring devotion to Mary under the title Help of Christians led him to build a great basilica in her honor in Turin.

The Salesian order he founded remains today one of the largest religious congregations in the Catholic Church, still guided by his conviction that young people are best formed not through fear, but through reason, religion, and kindness.
